claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit insufficient high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial refractory high-entropy alloy has heterogeneous surface conditions under high-temperature exposure.
A data-driven machine-learning model can determine optimal friction-processing or surface-treatment parameters for a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Existing high-throughput oxidation-test data can be used to optimize friction-processing parameters.
Machine-learning-optimized friction processing can enhance oxidation resistance in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Friction processing can improve oxidation resistance without modifying the alloy's bulk composition.
Isothermal oxidation at approximately 1000–1100°C is representative of high-temperature structural applications for these alloys.
Optimized friction processing produces a refined surface microstructure.
Optimized friction processing reduces surface defects.
A refined, defect-reduced surface facilitates formation of a homogeneous and adherent oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale may contain CrTaO4 or Al2O3.
Optimized friction processing removes surface defects.
Optimized friction processing refines grain boundaries at the surface.
Surface-defect removal and grain-boundary refinement enable formation of a more uniform and coherent protective oxide scale.
A uniform and coherent protective oxide scale acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen.
The oxygen diffusion barrier reduces further oxidation rates at high temperature.
Machine-learning-optimized friction processing will produce lower oxidation weight gain than conventional processing.
Machine-learning-optimized friction processing will improve oxide-scale uniformity and adhesion relative to conventional processing.
Standard processing methods produce higher and less controlled oxidation behavior than data-driven optimized processing.
The proposed method applies primarily where surface-treatment effects dominate over bulk-composition effects.
